idiom_name: hand-rolled tagged-union event struct + subscriber registry (or a C message-queue client)
implementation_notes: C supplies none of the three ingredients: no sum type, no reflection-based (de)serialisation and no channel primitive. The canonical realization is a struct whose first field is an enum tag - the event type id - followed by a union of payload structs, plus a hand-written encoder/decoder that writes the tag first (network byte order, explicit lengths) so a consumer can switch on it before touching payload bytes; delivery is a subscriber array of callbacks or a client for a queue/broker (POSIX mqueue, MQTT, AMQP). The union replaces the classic event class hierarchy and the tag switch replaces virtual dispatch, but both must be written by hand. Use this level of manual framing only when you truly need it; a small IDL (protobuf-c, FlatBuffers) or a broker client library that does the framing is usually less error-prone than hand-rolled encoding.
pitfalls: Reading a union member other than the one last written reinterprets the stored bytes (type punning): always switch on the tag and validate it before touching payload members.
memcpy()-ing the struct onto the wire embeds ABI padding; serialise field by field with explicit order, width and length prefixes, or pin the layout with a wire format.
A callback registry needs a policy for mutation and lifetime during dispatch: unsubscribing or freeing a handler while publishing is a use-after-free.

Nothing enforces that a new EV_* tag got a matching decoder branch: keep the enum, encoder, decoder and subscriber switch in one place so a missed case is a compile-time or table-driven failure, not a silent misparse.
